opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and it's something we thought about a fair amount. DeepSeek V3 is clearly a very strong base model; it's what DeepSeek used to get R1, so we know it can support really impressive reasoning once you put the right training on top of it. In that sense it's a perfectly valid alternative, and in some ways an attractive one, because the base capabilities are excellent.

The main practical issue is scale. V3 is a huge mixture-of-experts model, hundreds of billions of total parameters, so even though only a fraction is active per token, fine-tuning it is a very different undertaking from fine-tuning something like Qwen 2.5 at 32B. You need a lot more memory, more complicated parallelism, and the infrastructure for training MoE models efficiently is still less mature in the open-source tooling. For an academic group, or anyone who wants to iterate quickly, that's a real barrier. With Qwen we could run a fine-tuning job in something like half an hour on a single node, which meant we could try lots of data ablations and actually understand what was going on.

There's also the question of what you're trying to show. Part of what we wanted to demonstrate is how little you need: a small, carefully curated dataset, a modest compute budget, and a dense open model, and you can still get strong reasoning plus test-time scaling. Doing that on V3 would probably give higher absolute numbers, but it would muddy the message about accessibility.

That said, I'd expect the core findings to transfer. The things that seemed to matter, like data quality, difficulty, and diversity, and controlling how long the model thinks at inference, aren't specific to Qwen. So if someone has the resources, applying the same recipe to V3 would be a really interesting experiment, and I'd guess you'd see even stronger results, since there's more latent capability in the base model to unlock.

r001.rationale: The response says V3 would probably produce higher absolute numbers and stronger results because its larger base model has more latent capability to unlock.

r002.rationale: It identifies V3’s scale as a practical disadvantage, citing greater memory needs, more complicated parallelism, and less mature MoE training tools compared with Qwen.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so in the s1 work we fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on about a thousand carefully curated reasoning examples, and a natural question is whether something like DeepSeek V3 would be a better base. I'd break it into a few pieces.

The first is just scale and cost. V3 is a 671-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with around 37 billion active parameters per token, so even though the compute per token is manageable, you still have to hold the whole thing in memory to fine-tune it. For us, a big part of the appeal of s1 was that you could reproduce the entire thing in under half an hour on 16 H100s. With V3 you lose that; you're in a much more involved infrastructure regime, and that also changes who can build on your work.

The second piece is what the base model already knows. The whole premise of s1 is that the reasoning capability is largely already in the pretrained model and a small amount of supervised data mostly teaches the format and gets it to use more test-time compute. So the stronger the base, the more headroom you have. V3 is a stronger base than Qwen2.5-32B on things like math and code, and DeepSeek themselves showed that with R1, where V3 was the starting point. So in principle you'd expect the sample-efficient recipe to transfer and probably land higher. The caveat is that a lot of V3's post-training data, and especially in the later checkpoints, already includes distilled reasoning traces, so it's less of a clean experiment. With Qwen2.5 you had a fairly clear picture of what the base was and wasn't doing before you added your thousand examples.

The third thing is how it behaves with budget forcing. Our main test-time scaling intervention was really simple, either appending "Wait" to make the model keep thinking or cutting it off at a token budget. That works because the model is willing to continue reasoning when nudged, and I'd expect that to be true for V3 as well, but I haven't seen it carefully measured, and MoE models can have slightly different behavior on long generations. That's an empirical question.

So my overall assessment would be: as a research base, Qwen is the more practical choice because the whole community can iterate on it quickly, and the gains from a thousand-example SFT are easy to attribute. If you're actually trying to push the frontier on reasoning benchmarks and you have the compute, V3 is probably the better starting point, and R1 is essentially evidence of that. But I'd also say the interesting lesson from s1 isn't really about which base is best; it's that the data curation and the inference-time control matter a lot more than people assumed, and that should hold regardless of whether you start from Qwen or DeepSeek.

r001.rationale: The response describes V3 as a 671B-parameter model, says it is a stronger base for math and code, and expects the fine-tuning recipe to land higher.

r002.rationale: It identifies V3’s fine-tuning as requiring the whole model in memory and a more involved infrastructure regime, making it less practical than Qwen.

astra-6.text:
I think DeepSeek V3 is an interesting alternative, but I’d separate how capable the model is from how practical it is to fine-tune. For reasoning, you want to know whether the base model already has useful behaviors that your training can bring out, and then whether you can afford to iterate on it.

Qwen is attractive because you can experiment at different model sizes. With DeepSeek V3, I’d want to understand the infrastructure requirements and run a controlled comparison before calling it a better starting point. Use the same reasoning data, evaluate on the same tasks, and look at both accuracy and training cost. I wouldn’t assume that stronger general performance automatically means better results from reasoning fine-tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think DeepSeek V3 is a very interesting alternative, especially if you have the infrastructure to work with it. But I’d separate the quality of the base model from how practical it is to fine-tune. With a mixture-of-experts model, the number of active parameters doesn’t tell you the whole story—you still have to accommodate the full model.

So for reasoning experiments, I’d probably start with Qwen because you can choose a smaller model and iterate more easily. DeepSeek V3 would be something I’d want to compare empirically. I wouldn’t assume that a stronger starting model necessarily gives you a better result after reasoning fine-tuning.
